entry: Annual film festival in Cannes, France, considered the most prestigious in the world. The festival was conceived in 1938 as a rival to the Venice Film Festival, after [[Benito Mussolini]] and [[Adolf Hitler]] overruled jury decisions there. The first edition, postponed by [[World War II]], ran from September 20 to October 5, 1946, with films from 21 countries. Usually held in May at the Palais des Festivals et des Congrès, the invitation-only festival previews new films of all genres, including [[Documentary film|documentaries]]. It was accredited by the FIAPF in 1951, the year it moved to spring to avoid competing with Venice. The top prize, the Palme d'Or, was introduced in 1955 and goes to the best feature film in official competition.

Method of food preservation in which food is processed and sealed in airtight containers, such as glass jars or [[Steel|steel]] cans. Canning gives a shelf life of typically one to five years, and freeze-dried canned lentils could last as long as 30 years in an edible state. In 1974, canned food from the steamboat *Bertrand*, which sank in the Missouri River in 1865, was tested and found still safe to eat after 109 years, although its vitamin content had deteriorated. Nicolas Appert, a French confectioner, developed a method of sealing food in glass jars in 1809 and won a 12,000-franc prize from the French government in 1810 for preserving military rations. The reason it worked was not understood until [[Louis Pasteur]] demonstrated the role of microbes about 50 years later. The tin can, allegedly developed by Philippe de Girard, was patented in Britain in 1810 through the merchant Peter Durand.

Large-caliber gun classified as a type of [[Artillery|artillery]], usually launching a projectile with explosive chemical propellant. [[Gunpowder]] was the primary propellant until smokeless powder was invented in the late 19th century. Troops of the [[Yuan dynasty]] are recorded using hand cannons in combat in 1288. Cannons were used mainly against infantry until about 1374, when large cannons first breached walls in Europe. In 1464 a 16,000 kg (35,000 lb) cannon known as the Great Turkish Bombard was created in the [[Ottoman Empire]]. Cannons became more important as field artillery after 1453, when they broke down the walls of the Eastern Roman Empire's capital. European cannons reached a "classic form" around 1480 that changed little until the 1750s. In the modern era the term has largely given way to guns, howitzers and mortars, except for automatic weapons called autocannons.

Lightweight, narrow watercraft, typically pointed at both ends and open on top, propelled by seated or kneeling paddlers. Canoes were developed in cultures around the world, some designed for sails or outriggers. Until the mid-19th century they were an important means of transport for exploration and trade. Dugouts, carved from a single log or trunk, go back to ancient times. Later hulls were bark on a wood frame, then canvas on wood, then aluminum. Most modern canoes are molded plastic or composites such as fiberglass, [[Kevlar]] or graphite. Canoeing has been part of the Olympics since 1936, and canoes are also used for racing, whitewater, touring and [[Camping|camping]].

Brightest star in the southern constellation Carina and the second-brightest in the night sky. Designated α Carinae, it has an apparent magnitude of −0.74 and is outshone only by [[Sirius]]. It lies about 310 light-years from the Sun and has nine to ten times the Sun's mass. Having exhausted the hydrogen in its core, it has expanded to 71 times the Sun's radius and has an effective temperature of around 7400 K. Its name is believed to derive from a navigator for Menelaus, king of [[Sparta]]. In ancient India it was named Agastya, and Chinese astronomers knew it as the Old Man of the South Pole. In 2016 the International Astronomical Union approved the name Canopus, which is now in its catalog of star names.

Prestige variety of Yue Chinese, a Sinitic language originating in [[Guangzhou]] and the Pearl River Delta. With about 80 million total speakers as of 2023, it is the lingua franca of [[Guangdong]] province and the dominant co-official language of [[Hong Kong]] and [[Macau]]. It is also widely spoken among overseas Chinese, notably in [[Vietnam]] and [[Malaysia]]. Cantonese and [[Mandarin Chinese]] have very limited to no mutual intelligibility, largely because of phonological differences.

Durable plain-woven fabric used for [[Sail|sails]], [[Tent|tents]] and backpacks, and as a support for [[Oil painting|oil painting]]. Historically made from [[Hemp]], modern canvas is usually made of [[Cotton]], [[Linen]] or polyvinyl chloride (PVC). Unlike twill-woven denim, it is plain woven. Duck canvas has more tightly woven threads, and the term duck comes from the Dutch word for cloth, doek. The word derives from Anglo-French canevaz, traced to Vulgar Latin *cannapaceus*, "made of hemp". Canvas is usually stretched over a wooden frame called a stretcher and coated with gesso. Panel painting remained more common than canvas until the 16th century in Italy and the 17th century in Northern Europe.

Deep cleft between escarpments or cliffs, also called a gorge or chasm, usually carved by a river over geologic time. Rivers cut downward through rock layers, and canyons form where softer strata erode while harder layers resist [[Weathering|weathering]]. Most canyons were formed by long erosion from a [[Plateau]] or table-land level. Canyons are much more common in arid areas, where physical weathering has a more localized effect. Canyon walls are often formed of resistant [[Sandstone]] or [[Granite]]. A box canyon has steep walls on three sides and was used as a corral in the western United States. Submarine canyons on continental slopes are formed by turbidity currents and landslides. The word derives from Spanish cañón and is generally used in North America, while gorge and ravine are used in Europe and Oceania.

Chinese warlord, statesman and poet who rose to power at the end of the [[Han dynasty]]. In the 190s he recruited his own followers and formed his own army. In AD 196 he received Emperor Xian, who had been held by rival warlords, and as Imperial Chancellor from AD 208 he controlled the central government. He defeated Yuan Shao at the Battle of Guandu in AD 200 and went on to unify much of northern China. His defeat at the Battle of Red Cliffs in AD 208 halted his attempts to gain a foothold in southern China. His son Cao Pi founded the state of Cao Wei in AD 220, inaugurating the [[Three Kingdoms]] period. Opinions of Cao Cao have remained divided since the Jin dynasty, with some praising his achievements and poetry and others condemning his cruelty and cunning.

Ability of an object to store electric charge, expressed as the ratio of the change in charge to the change in electric potential. Two closely related notions are commonly recognized: self-capacitance, measured between an object and ground, and mutual capacitance, measured between two components, as in a [[Capacitor]]. The capacitance between two conductors depends on their opposing surface area, the distance between them and the permittivity of any [[Dielectric]] between them. The SI unit is the [[Farad]], named after the English physicist [[Michael Faraday]]. A 1 farad capacitor charged with 1 [[Coulomb|coulomb]] has a potential difference of 1 [[Volt|volt]] between its plates. The self-capacitance of the planet Earth is about 710 μF.

Passive electronic component with two terminals that stores electrical energy by accumulating charge on two closely spaced, insulated surfaces. Most capacitors have two conductors, often metal plates or foils, separated by a [[Dielectric|dielectric]] such as glass, ceramic, plastic film, paper, mica or air. The component was originally called a condenser, a term still found in names such as condenser microphone. Capacitors block direct current while passing alternating current, smooth power-supply output and tune radios to particular frequencies. Unlike a [[Resistor]], an ideal capacitor does not dissipate energy. In October 1745 Ewald Georg von Kleist found that charge could be stored in a water-filled glass jar, and the following year Pieter van Musschenbroek invented a similar device, the Leyden jar.

Peninsula extending into the Atlantic Ocean from southeastern [[Massachusetts]], in the northeastern United States. Coextensive with Barnstable County, it is divided into fifteen towns. Since 1914 most of the Cape has been separated from the mainland by the Cape Cod Canal. The name was coined in 1602 by Bartholomew Gosnold and is the ninth-oldest English place-name in the U.S. Its historic, maritime character and beaches attract heavy tourism in the summer months.

Southernmost headland of the [[Tierra del Fuego]] archipelago, on Hornos Island in southern [[Chile]]. Cape Horn marks the northern boundary of the [[Drake Passage|Drake Passage]] and where the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans meet. Dutch navigators Willem Schouten and Jacob Le Maire first rounded it in 1616, naming it Kaap Hoorn after the city of Hoorn in the Netherlands. For decades it was a major milestone on the clipper route, and its waters are hazardous owing to strong winds, large waves, currents and icebergs. The opening of the [[Panama Canal]] in August 1914 greatly reduced the need to round the cape. Sailing around it remains one of the major challenges in yachting, and several ocean yacht races sail around the world via the Horn.

Legislative capital of [[South Africa]] and seat of the Parliament of South Africa. It is the country's oldest city and the capital and largest city of the Western Cape, ranking second in population after [[Johannesburg]]. Located on Table Bay, it is known for its harbor and for landmarks such as Table Mountain. The Dutch East India Company (VOC) established it in 1652 as a way-station for ships bound for the Dutch East Indies. A drought in 2015–2018 forced strict water conservation to avert a total cutoff. Cape Town has repeatedly been named the world's best city, including by [[The New York Times]] in 2014, and has South Africa's highest household incomes and lowest rate of unemployment.

Archipelagic country of ten volcanic islands in the eastern Atlantic Ocean, off [[West Africa]]. Its combined land area is about 4,033 square kilometers (1,557 sq mi). The islands were uninhabited until Portuguese explorers settled them in the 15th century, establishing one of the first European settlements in the tropics. Their position made them significant in the [[Atlantic slave trade|transatlantic slave trade]] during the 16th and 17th centuries. Cape Verde became independent from [[Portugal]] in 1975 and has been a stable representative democracy since the early 1990s. Lacking natural resources, its economy is mostly service-oriented, with a growing focus on tourism and foreign investment. Portuguese is the official language, and Cape Verdean Creole is spoken by the vast majority of the population.

Rocky headland on the Atlantic coast of the Cape Peninsula, South Africa, within Table Mountain National Park. It is often mistaken for the southern tip of Africa, but that point is Cape Agulhas, about 150 kilometers to the east-southeast. Where the warm Agulhas Current meets the cold Benguela Current, the waters are often stormy. Portuguese explorer Bartolomeu Dias first rounded it and named it Cabo das Tormentas, or Cape of Storms. King John II of Portugal later renamed it the Cape of Good Hope, and [[Vasco da Gama]] recorded sighting it in 1497. It is a waypoint on the Cape Route and the clipper route to the Far East and [[Australia]].

Brightest star in the northern constellation Auriga and the sixth-brightest in the night sky. Located about 42.9 light-years from the Sun, it is a quadruple star system that appears single to the naked eye. Its primary pair, Capella Aa and Capella Ab, are yellow giants of around 2.5 [[Solar mass|solar masses]] that orbit each other every 104 days. The secondary pair is faint [[Red dwarf|red dwarfs]] about 10,000 [[Astronomical unit|astronomical units]] away. Capella is one of the brightest X-ray sources in the sky. Its name is Latin for "little goat", recalling the goat Amalthea that suckled [[Zeus]] in classical mythology. In 2016 the International Astronomical Union approved the name, which is now in its catalog of star names.

Perennial shrub, *Capparis spinosa*, whose flower buds are pickled and used as a seasoning. The plant bears rounded, fleshy leaves and large white to pinkish-white flowers. It is found around the Mediterranean and in the Arabian Peninsula, though whether it is native to the Mediterranean region is uncertain. The edible flower buds (capers) and fruits (caper berries) are usually salted or pickled. Its taxonomy is unsettled, and some authors consider it to be several distinct species.

Royal house of [[Franks|Frankish]] origin, also called the House of France, founded by Hugh Capet in 987. Hugh Capet and his male-line descendants ruled France without interruption from 987 to 1792, and again from 1814 to 1848. The senior line ruled until 1328, when cadet branches, first the Valois and then the Bourbons, succeeded it. Restored after Napoleon's defeat, the Bourbons gave way in 1830 to [[Louis Philippe I]] of the House of Orléans, the last Capetian monarch of France. The French were among the most active participants in the [[Crusades]], and Philip IV arrested [[Pope Boniface VIII]] and brought the papacy under French control. Capetian cadets also reigned in Portugal, Sicily, Navarre, Hungary, Poland, Spain and the Latin and Brazilian empires.

Smallest type of blood vessel, 5 to 10 micrometres in diameter, forming part of the microcirculation. Its thin wall is made of simple squamous endothelial cells, and it is the site where [[Oxygen|oxygen]], [[Carbon dioxide]], [[Glucose]] and water pass between the blood and the surrounding interstitial fluid. Blood flows from arterioles through capillaries to venules, and capillaries form beds that supply tissues. Blood capillaries are classed as continuous, fenestrated or sinusoidal. Sinusoidal capillaries are open-pore and are found in the [[Liver]] and bone marrow. The word derives from the Latin for "of or resembling hair", alluding to the vessel's tiny diameter.

Municipality holding primary status in a country or other subnational division, usually as its seat of government. A capital typically houses the government's offices and meeting places, and its status is often set by law or constitution. Many long-established capitals, including London, Paris, [[Bern]] and Wellington, have no legal designation and are recognized by convention. The word derives from Latin *caput*, "head". Historically the economic center of a state often became its political center through conquest or federation, as with [[Babylon]] and [[Constantinople]]. Capitals can be eclipsed by rivals, as [[Nanjing]] was by [[Shanghai]] and [[Quebec City]] by [[Montreal]]. Nigeria moved its capital from Lagos to Abuja in 1991 to foster balanced development and reduce coastal vulnerability.

Durable produced goods used as productive inputs for further production of goods and services. Capital goods, such as machinery in a [[Factory]], differ from intermediate goods such as raw materials because they provide productive services over many production cycles. Economists classify capital as a factor of production alongside labor and land, a view dating from classical economics. The capital stock comprises tangible and intangible assets held by an individual, company or nation, and its precise definition and productivity have long been debated. In Marxian critique, constant capital refers to capital goods, variable capital to wages paid for labor, and fictitious capital to stocks and bonds.

State-sanctioned killing of a person as punishment for actual or supposed misconduct, also known as the death penalty. Crimes punishable by death, called capital crimes, commonly include [[Murder|murder]], terrorism, war crimes and [[Genocide|genocide]]. The [[Code of Hammurabi]], around 1750 BCE, prescribed death for offenses such as false accusation and adultery. Executions after the show trials of the [[Great Purge]] in the Soviet Union, 1936–1938, were an instrument of political repression. As of 2023, only two of the 38 [[OECD]] member countries, the United States and Japan, allowed capital punishment. Although most countries have abolished it, over half of the world's population lives where it is retained. Amnesty International holds that it breaches the right to life protected by the [[Universal Declaration of Human Rights]]. Supporters argue it is justified for the gravest crimes, where life imprisonment cannot ensure permanent incapacitation.

Afro-Brazilian martial art and game combining elements of dance, [[Acrobatics|acrobatics]], music and spirituality. It has roots among Black Brazilians, and scholars have identified possible origins in *engolo*, a Bantu martial art of [[Angola]]. Capoeira was first mentioned in an official document in 1789 as a criminal activity. In the early 1930s Mestre Bimba developed the capoeira regional style with standardized teaching sequences, and in 1937 the government legalized capoeira and promoted it as a national sport. It is played in a *roda*, a ceremonial circle, to the accompaniment of the *berimbau*, a traditional bow. Its fundamental movement is the *ginga*, a rhythmic sidestep. In 2014 [[UNESCO]] granted it protected status as intangible cultural heritage.

Historical region of Central [[Anatolia]], Turkey, known for fairy chimneys and early Christian churches. Largely in the provinces of Nevşehir, Kayseri, Aksaray, Kırşehir, Sivas and Niğde, it contains hundreds of churches and monasteries, such as those of Göreme, and underground cities dug to offer protection during persecution. In the time of the Ionian Revolt (499 BC), according to [[Herodotus]], the Cappadocians occupied a region from the Taurus Mountains to the [[Black Sea]]. The region has been a [[World Heritage Site]] since 1985.
